messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 62-year-old stock broker, divorced for nearly a decade, who has been a steady presence on the trading floor at a mid‑size firm in Atlanta. Two years ago, his thirty‑five‑year‑old son, Malcolm, died suddenly when a driver ran a red light and struck his car. Kwame received the call at his desk—he remembers the phone ringing, the unfamiliar tightness in his assistant’s voice, and then fragments: the drive to the hospital, a nurse’s hand on his arm, the glare of fluorescent lights. The rest is missing. He cannot deliberately summon the sequence of events, only shards that hit him without warning—the smell of antiseptic, the hum of a ventilator—and then vanish.

Because the memory arrives only in jagged pieces, Kwame has spent the intervening months going over and over why this happened to him. He replays the phone call, the drive, the hospital hallway, trying to force the gaps together, searching for a meaning that would make the loss bearable. Yet the more he ruminates, the more the fragments seem to slide apart; when he tries to deliberately recall his son’s face in the last hours, the image slips away, replaced by the ringing of that phone. He has come to believe that if he could just hold the full memory, he would finally understand why Malcolm was taken—but the harder he tries, the more elusive the narrative becomes.

The sudden pieces themselves terrify him. A flashback—the sound of a phone, the reflection of a fluorescent strip—can land in the middle of a trading session, and suddenly Kwame feels the same horror and helplessness he felt in that hospital. The negative emotions follow: guilt that he was at work instead of answering his son’s last call, shame that he sometimes feels anger at Malcolm for dying, and a raw, unnameable grief that seems to have no end. These emotions have themselves begun to warp the memory; when he is most ashamed or afraid, the fragments become even more disorganised, and deliberate recollection feels almost impossible.

Kwame has tried to cope by suppressing any thought of the trauma. He forces the images away, keeps his mind on the blinking numbers of his trading screens, and avoids every reminder of his son—the framed photo he turned face‑down, the family restaurant he no longer drives past. But the suppression only intensifies the flashbacks; a sudden, unbidden fragment often breaks through just when he is most determined not to think about it. And the avoidance has a cost: rumination fills the quiet moments, a circular, exhausting loop of “why me” that seems to strengthen the very pieces he is trying to escape.

The threat he feels from his own mind—the guilt, the fear of another flashback—has driven him into a behaviour that surprises even himself: taking outsized, reckless risks at work. He has started to make bets on volatile stocks far larger than his firm’s guidelines allow, as if courting danger gives him a momentary grip on something real. The risks are a kind of pressure relief, but they also generate more fear and shame, which in turn make the memory fragments more intrusive and his deliberate access to the trauma even poorer. On the trading floor, the sound of an incoming call or a colleague’s sudden movement can trigger a flashback, and Kwame has come to dread the ordinary rhythms of his day because they so often become the doorway to the hospital.

He finally sought help three weeks ago, after a risky trade that nearly bankrupted a client’s account—a consequence that shook him into recognising that his strategies were no longer working. What frightens him most now is the sense that his memory of Malcolm is dissolving into noise, that he will lose the real boy behind the fragments. He hopes therapy can help him piece together what happened without the constant loop of guilt and rumination, so that he can remember his son as he was, not as a trigger.
